conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time for this today. I’m Jennifer, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. The EPDS is simply 10 questions about the past week; it isn’t a test of your parenting, and there are no right or wrong answers. Everything we discuss stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and we’ll go at whatever pace feels comfortable for you. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft sigh, eyes down]  
Honestly… not very often. I used to laugh a lot before the baby—little things would crack me up—but this week, even when my husband tried to joke about the diaper explosions, I mostly just forced a tiny smile. It feels like the joy is stuck behind a wall or something. I’ll maybe get a quick laugh once, but then it fades right away and I’m back to feeling flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod]  
Yeah… that’s pretty much what I just said. I can still laugh, but it’s rare and it doesn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]  
Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still go through the motions, hoping maybe I’ll feel something, but it’s like the spark is gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes flick toward the floor, voice tight]  
Yeah… a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him right. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every tiny choice I’d made, convinced it was my fault. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the guilt still sits heavy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Pretty much all the time. My heart’s racing the second I open my eyes. I’ll check that he’s breathing, then five minutes later I’m leaning over the crib again sure something’s wrong—even though nothing happened. There’s this loop in my head: “What if he spits up and chokes? What if I fall asleep while feeding him?” I can’t shut it off, even when everything’s perfectly fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
Yes… a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and for a minute I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. Night before last I was just folding laundry and it hit me out of nowhere; I had to sit down and grip the couch cushions until the feeling passed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly, shoulders sag]  
Most of the time it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. A couple of dishes in the sink or one extra diaper change and it’s like the whole day collapses on me. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but I end up staring at the mess with this heavy, frozen feeling, wondering how everyone else does it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods, eyes glassy]  
Yeah. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning— replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up, worrying about the next feed, the next cry. I’ll drift off eventually, then jolt awake sure I heard him, even when he’s quiet. Most nights this week I’ve been awake at least an hour or two before I can settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet voice, eyes on the floor]  
Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start sliding down without warning. I feel empty, like I’m watching life through a window instead of really being in it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, nods]  
Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week. Not little sniffles—full-on sobbing in the bathroom because everything felt too heavy. I try to stop before my husband hears; I don’t want him worrying more than he already does.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice shaky]  
…once or twice. It’s just a quick flash—like, “What if I weren’t here, then maybe everyone else could rest.” I haven’t made any plans or anything, and I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thought sneaks in when I’m at my lowest. It scares me, and I push it away as fast as it comes.

You've shared that over the past week laughter comes only rarely and fades quickly, activities you used to anticipate now feel empty, and you blame yourself whenever your baby fusses. You described constant <sym>worry</sym>, sudden <sym>panic</sym>, feeling overwhelmed by tiny tasks, nightly restless sleep filled with racing thoughts, daily <sym>sadness</sym> and spontaneous tears, and brief frightening thoughts that everyone might be better off without you. These feelings are understandably heavy, and they do not reflect any failing on your part-many new mothers experience similar struggles, and help is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is now rare and fleeting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory joy—'nothing feels worth looking forward to' and 'the spark is gone'—which aligns with 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame that intrudes despite rational awareness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, racing anxiety unrelated to actual events, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden multiple episodes of intense physical panic (tight chest, shakes, dread) without identifiable cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent overwhelm, inability to handle routine tasks, and feeling 'drowned' by minor demands, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption from racing anxious thoughts and repeated awakenings, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, tearfulness without trigger, and emotional detachment, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes full-on sobbing twice this week due to feeling overwhelmed, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 or any positive response on EPDS item 10 signals probable <med>postpartum depression</med>; your score of 25 exceeds this threshold. You endorse ≥5 key symptoms (low mood, loss of interest, guilt, concentration difficulty, suicidal ideation) required by <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, most days for >2 weeks, causing impairment. Frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> symptoms suggest co-morbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. The presence of <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym>, even if fleeting, mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>obstetric provider</med> to discuss these results and create a safety plan
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> (psychiatrist or therapist) for full evaluation and evidence-based treatment options
3. Call a trusted friend, family member, or neighbour today so you are not alone with the baby until medical review; share how low you are feeling
4. If thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe, contact emergency services (911) or go to nearest emergency department
5. Begin gentle daily structure: one 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced meals, and accept help with household tasks or night-time bottles
6. Practice short <med>breathing exercises</med>: inhale 4 s, hold 4 s, exhale 6 s when <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes; repeat 10 cycles
7. Keep the baby's crib or bassinet within arm's reach for night feeds to reduce fatigue from getting up
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report on EPDS-10 items

Symptoms endorsed
- Marked anhedonia (loss of pleasure/interest)  
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt about infant care  
- Unremitting, intrusive worries (breathing, choking, “doing it wrong”)  
- Discrete panic episodes (tight chest, trembling) without clear trigger  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; functional “freeze”  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to rumination  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“flash” thoughts of not wanting to be here; no plan, no intent)

Pattern summary  
Patient describes a 2-week (or longer) period of low mood, anhedonia, guilt, and anxiety that cluster with the postpartum period. Symptoms are present most of the time, interfere with daily functioning, and are distressing to her.

Risk flags  
- Passive suicidal ideation → safety concern  
- Moderate–severe anxiety with panic features  
- Significant subjective impairment in caretaking confidence

Screening impression  
Responses meet threshold indicators for possible major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Recommend immediate formal psychiatric evaluation, safety plan, and consideration of expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty team.
